subject: geography
title: KS3 Geography - Industry and Economic Activity
subtitle: Employment sectors, location factors, supply chains, UK economic change and tourism impacts.
description: A KS3 geography revision pack on how people make a living, where economic activities happen, and how industry changes over time. It covers employment sectors, industrial location, supply chains, deindustrialisation, tourism impacts, sustainable tourism and data skills.

data.targetWord: work that produces goods or services

examples.en-GB: Economic activity includes farming, manufacturing, teaching, transport and tourism.

data.targetWord: physical products that can be bought and sold

examples.en-GB: Cars, bread, phones and clothes are examples of goods.

data.targetWord: work done for people or businesses

examples.en-GB: Healthcare, teaching, banking, transport and tourism are services.

data.targetWord: a category used to group jobs by the type of work they involve

examples.en-GB: Primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary are the four main employment sectors.

data.targetWord: work that extracts or collects raw materials from the natural environment

examples.en-GB: Farming, fishing, forestry, mining and quarrying are primary sector activities.

data.targetWord: work that manufactures or processes raw materials into products

examples.en-GB: Car manufacturing, food processing, steel making and construction are secondary sector activities.

data.targetWord: work that provides services to people or businesses

examples.en-GB: Retail, healthcare, education, transport and banking are tertiary sector activities.

data.targetWord: work based on knowledge, research, information and high-level technology

examples.en-GB: Software design, robotics, scientific research and data analysis are quaternary sector activities.

data.targetWord: natural resources used to make products

examples.en-GB: Wood, cotton, oil, coal, iron ore and fish are raw materials.

data.targetWord: making products, usually in factories

examples.en-GB: A clothing factory is involved in manufacturing because it makes products.

data.targetWord: a type of economic activity

examples.en-GB: Farming, car making, tourism and finance are different industries.

data.targetWord: the percentage of workers employed in each economic sector

examples.en-GB: Employment structure can show whether an economy is mainly primary, industrial, service-based or knowledge-based.

data.targetWord: the decline in the importance of manufacturing and heavy industry in an economy

examples.en-GB: Deindustrialisation affected UK coal mining, steel making, shipbuilding and textiles.

data.targetWord: the use of machines, robots or computer systems to do work that people used to do

examples.en-GB: Automation can reduce the number of workers needed for repetitive factory tasks.

data.targetWord: the increasing connections between countries through trade, transport, technology, finance and culture

examples.en-GB: Globalisation allows companies to make, ship and sell products across many countries.

data.targetWord: a reason why an industry chooses to locate in a particular place

examples.en-GB: Raw materials, labour, transport, market, land cost and energy are location factors.

data.targetWord: the customers who buy a product or service

examples.en-GB: A bakery may locate near its market so bread can be sold quickly to local customers.

data.targetWord: workers available for employment

examples.en-GB: A factory needs access to labour so it can employ enough workers.

data.targetWord: workers with training, qualifications or specialist knowledge

examples.en-GB: High-tech industries often need skilled labour from universities and research centres.

data.targetWord: basic systems that help places function, such as roads, ports, electricity, broadband and water supply

examples.en-GB: Good infrastructure helps businesses move goods, contact customers and access energy.

data.targetWord: an industry that is not strongly tied to one location because it can operate in many places

examples.en-GB: Software design can be footloose, but it may still need skilled workers, broadband and airports.

data.targetWord: the sequence of stages involved in making and selling a product

examples.en-GB: A T-shirt supply chain may include cotton growing, spinning, sewing, shipping, retail and recycling.

data.targetWord: moving goods from one place to another

examples.en-GB: Distribution links factories, warehouses, ports, shops and customers.

data.targetWord: travel away from home for leisure, business, culture, sport, shopping or adventure

examples.en-GB: Tourism supports jobs in hotels, restaurants, transport, shops, museums and national parks.

data.targetWord: something that encourages people to visit a place

examples.en-GB: Beaches, mountains, castles, museums, festivals and sports stadiums can be tourist attractions.

data.targetWord: when money spent in one business supports further jobs and income in other businesses

examples.en-GB: A hotel pays staff and buys local food, helping wages and spending circulate locally.

data.targetWord: changes in activity during different times of the year

examples.en-GB: A coastal resort may have high visitor numbers in summer and fewer visitors in winter.

data.targetWord: tourism managed so that it supports local people and protects the environment for the future

examples.en-GB: Sustainable tourism may include visitor limits, public transport, footpath repairs and local guides.

data.targetWord: tourism focused on nature conservation, local benefits and low environmental impact

examples.en-GB: Costa Rica is often used as an example of ecotourism because of its national parks, wildlife and local guides.

data.targetWord: work that is not officially recorded, taxed or protected by formal employment rules

examples.en-GB: Street vending, casual cleaning and unregistered market trading can be part of the informal economy.

data.targetWord: a UK example of an area affected by coal mining decline and deindustrialisation

examples.en-GB: The South Wales coalfield shows how the decline of one industry can affect jobs, shops, services and community life.

data.targetWord: a UK example of a traditional steel industry affected by automation and global competition

examples.en-GB: Sheffield still has advanced manufacturing, but steel employment is much smaller than in the past.

data.targetWord: a UK example of textile growth during the Industrial Revolution followed by mill closures and urban change

examples.en-GB: Manchester grew as a textile city because cotton, canals, railways, workers and investment helped mills develop.

data.targetWord: a UK port area changed by containerisation, dock closure and regeneration

examples.en-GB: London Docklands regeneration created offices, housing, transport improvements and Canary Wharf.

data.targetWord: the high-tech cluster around Cambridge linked to research, skilled graduates and innovation

examples.en-GB: Silicon Fen is linked to software, biotechnology, electronics, research and the University of Cambridge.

data.targetWord: an area of economic growth along the M4 motorway with technology, offices, distribution and services

examples.en-GB: The M4 corridor benefits from motorway access, Heathrow Airport, links to London, skilled labour and business parks.

data.targetWord: a global manufacturing example that creates jobs but raises questions about wages, working conditions and pollution

examples.en-GB: Bangladesh exports clothing for global brands, especially from cities such as Dhaka and Chittagong.

data.targetWord: a UK tourism example with jobs and conservation benefits but problems such as erosion, congestion and second homes

examples.en-GB: The Lake District attracts visitors with mountains, lakes, walking routes, villages, wildlife and literary links.

data.title: Basic Product Supply Chain
data.instruction: Put the stages of a basic product supply chain in the correct order.
items: Raw materials are collected or grown.
Materials are processed into usable forms.
Components or products are manufactured.
Goods are transported and distributed.
Products are sold in shops or online.
The customer uses the product.
The product or packaging is repaired, reused, recycled or thrown away.

data.title: Tourism Multiplier Effect
data.instruction: Put the stages of the tourism multiplier effect in the correct order.
items: A tourist spends money at a local hotel.
The hotel pays staff and buys food from local suppliers.
Staff spend some of their wages in nearby shops.
Local shops order more goods and may employ workers.
More income and jobs are created in the local area.

data.title: Typical Employment Structure Change
data.instruction: Put the broad stages of employment structure change in order.
items: Many people work in primary jobs such as farming, fishing and mining.
Industrialisation increases secondary jobs in factories and construction.
Automation and global competition reduce some manufacturing employment.
Rising incomes increase demand for services such as healthcare, retail and leisure.
Education and technology help quaternary jobs in research, IT and data grow.

data.title: Industrial Location Decision
data.instruction: Put the location decision steps in a sensible order.
items: Identify what the business makes or provides.
Check whether raw materials are heavy, bulky or perishable.
Compare access to labour, skilled workers, transport and markets.
Consider energy, land costs, water, broadband and government support.
Choose the location with the best balance of cost and access.

examples.en-GB: Outsourcing reduces costs for companies.

data.targetWord: industry involving advanced technology and research

examples.en-GB: Biotechnology and aerospace are high-tech industries.

examples.en-GB: Science parks encourage collaboration between business and academia.

data.targetWord: a company operating in several countries

examples.en-GB: Many multinational companies seek the cheapest locations for manufacturing.

data.targetWord: a natural resource used in manufacturing

examples.en-GB: Steel mills were located near coal and iron ore deposits.

data.targetWord: the provision of electricity and fuel for industry

examples.en-GB: Reliable energy supply is essential for most industries.

data.targetWord: the availability of workers in an area

examples.en-GB: Skilled labour supply attracts high-tech industries.

data.targetWord: the road, rail, port, and airport connections of a location

examples.en-GB: Good transport links are essential for distributing goods.

data.targetWord: money available for investment in industry

examples.en-GB: Capital is needed to build factories and buy machinery.

data.targetWord: the tools, machines, and systems used in production

examples.en-GB: Technology allows more to be produced with fewer workers.

data.targetWord: the use of machines to perform tasks previously done by humans

examples.en-GB: Robotics has transformed manufacturing efficiency.

data.targetWord: the use of computers and networks to manage information

examples.en-GB: Information technology is central to the quaternary sector.
